p: MediMove - testing a medical startup idea with real users

As an expat managing my own healthcare, I kept running into the same friction: every time I switched doctors or countries, I had to dig up old records, translate them, and re-explain my medical history from scratch.
There was no single place to keep this information accessible and understandable across borders.
I started by mapping my own pain, then ran 5 informal interviews with other expats to see if the problem was shared. It was.
Expats need a centralized, language-agnostic way to store and share their health records with new providers. Rather than building the full product, I tested demand first.  Goal:
Over one month: 108 landing page views, 10 signups via the form — validating that the problem resonates enough to warrant further product development.

p: Redesigning a careers experience for a digital banking team
A large bank wanted to strengthen its employer brand among developers and digital specialists.
The career page was outdated and not built for a technical audience — it buried vacancies in generic HR content and didn’t reflect the actual digital team culture.
To collect visual references, I used the adjective method. It starts with four questions: what makes us different, what the visual identity should and shouldn’t communicate, and what our mission is.
Based on the answers, we define 4 adjectives that set the direction for the mood board.

Within one week, I designed a concept from scratch, tailored it to the target audience, and got it approved by 3 teams — built entirely on existing design system components, with no new development required

p: Kubernetes gives teams flexibility in running applications, but setting up an environment can involve infrastructure concepts developers don't work with every day
Can developers get more autonomy without sacrificing the infrastructure control platform teams need?
I focused on the moment when a team already has an application and needs an environment where it can be deployed
A lot time to spent to set up for each apllication
Platform teams define safe defaults; developers configure what matters to them
Might created a lot of templates
Projects list. The developer opens the list of their team’s projects and clicks “Create project”
Basics. They enter a project name and pick the environment: production, staging or development
Template. They pick a template. The platform team already set what’s inside, so the developer doesn’t configure infrastructure by hand
Resources. They set CPU, memory and storage. Values stay inside the template’s limits, and they can change them later
Access. They add teams and give each a role, like Developer or Viewer
Creating. The platform sets up the project, and the developer can close the page. They get a notification when it’s ready
Done. The project is ready, and the next step is to deploy the first application
I used templates instead of manual setup, so developers make fewer infrastructure decisions. Platform teams still control the defaults and policies.
Explain constraints instead of blocking users
When a value is over the limit, I don’t show a generic error. I explain why, and offer two ways out: use the maximum or ask for a higher limit.
Setup can fail halfway. I show which steps are done, what failed and why, and that nothing is left half-created. Retry continues from the failed step.
Can developers create a valid project without assistance?
How long does it take to go from setup to a ready project?
Where do users fail validation or misunderstand constraints?

p: From Support Tickets to Design Fix: Debit Card Discoverability
Business goal: map all user pain points across the full user journey before scaling the limited card collection
Problem: users frequently contacted support because they couldn’t find the page listing all limited edition cards
Create script and tasks together with another designer

Hello! Thank you for agreeing to participate in our research. My name is ______, I'm a product designer at Alfa-Bank. We're currently working on launching banking products with limited-edition designs, and it's important for us to understand how easy and intuitive it is for people to find and order such products.

During the interview I'll give you some small tasks, then ask questions about what you saw and how you experienced it. We're evaluating the interface, not you — so there are no wrong answers. Please think out loud and don't hesitate to share any comments — it all helps us improve the service.

The study will take approximately 40 minutes. We'll be recording the screen and audio so we don't miss your impressions and can use them to improve the service. These recordings are not shared externally and are used only within the team. Is that okay with you?
Any questions, or shall we begin?
How old are you, and what city do you live in?
What do you do? What is your job title?
Which banks do you currently use? Which is your primary one and why?
How often do you use a physical card to pay?
Do you pay attention to the design of your bank card?
Do you buy items or products in limited-edition designs / collaborations with well-known brands or artists?

"Imagine you've just heard that Alfa-Bank has launched limited-edition banking products with various designs — collaborations with artists, brands, etc. Your task is to find such cards or stickers the way you would do it in real life."
Note: do not share the URL in advance — give the task, not the direct path.
Task 1: Find the Limited-Edition Cards and Stickers
"Try to find limited-edition products with designs. Act the way you normally would when looking for a new product or service."
Note: do not mention cards and stickers explicitly upfront.
Does the participant go to a search engine ("limited cards", "card design", "bank card", etc.)
Does the participant navigate to the Bank website manually
Does the participant search via mobile suggestions, hints, or ad blocks
Does the participant land on the card catalogue or promo page on their own
Does the participant notice the "Bank-Card with Engraving" section in the menu or catalogue
Does the participant use the on-site search
Why did you decide to start there?
What did you expect to see?
Did that path feel logical to you?
If the participant reaches the catalogue:
"Choose the card or sticker design you like most."
How the participant chooses among the visuals
Whether the participant navigates the catalogue cards
Whether the participant finds stickers with a design
Whether the participant understands the difference between a card and a sticker
Why did you choose that one?
Were there any difficulties finding the design you wanted?
Task 3: Go to the Product Page
"Explore the detailed information about the design product you selected."
How the participant navigates to the page
Whether the participant perceives it as a limited-edition product
Whether the participant notices information about the design, price, and features
"Look at the product information. Tell us what matters to you and what you see here."
Whether the participant understands how to switch between designs
Where the participant looks for pricing / tariffs
How the participant interprets the terms
"Imagine you've decided to apply for the product you selected. Begin the application process. You may enter fictional details."
Whether the participant understands how to apply for the specific design they chose
Whether the participant easily finds the form
What do you think happens next?
How easy was it to find the limited-edition designs?
How did you find the design selection process overall?
Would you actually apply for a card with a design for yourself?
Tell us what you liked and didn't like. Was anything difficult?
Is there anything you'd like to add that I haven't asked about?
Note: if the participant did not reach the catalogue, at the end you can ask them to visit the page and comment on it.

«I just clicked the first link from the search results and started browsing — it didn’t even cross my mind that these could be old, archived cards. The page looked normal, so I assumed everything I was seeing was still available to order»

When transferred to a new team, I handed off a detailed research document including prioritised growth opportunities and design references
